evals.name: cost-floor-derivation
evals.prompt: Our video transcoding pipeline runs about 9,000 hours of source video a month and costs us roughly $47k/month on AWS MediaConvert. Finance has told us to get it under $20k by Q3. Every time I bring it up the platform team says that's just what transcoding costs at our volume and the only lever is a committed-use discount. I don't buy it but I don't know how to argue with them. Where do I even start?
evals.expected_output: Derives an irreducible cost floor (compute-seconds/CPU cost of the encode itself, e.g. self-hosted ffmpeg on spot instances), computes the multiple against the current $47k, attributes the gap to named factors (vendor margin, per-minute pricing model, redundant renditions, unwatched output), and orders the attack biggest-term-first rather than jumping to the committed-use discount.
expectations: Derives an explicit irreducible cost floor for the transcoding work itself (e.g. raw compute cost of encoding 9,000 hours on self-managed/spot instances) and shows a concrete dollar figure or per-hour rate for it
States the multiple between the current $47k/month and the derived floor as an explicit ratio (e.g. 'about 6x')

Attributes the gap to specific named contributors (vendor margin, per-minute billing model, redundant renditions in the ABR ladder, transcoding assets nobody watches) rather than giving generic cost-cutting tips
Explicitly pushes back on the committed-use discount as the primary lever, on the grounds that a percentage off an unexamined number cannot reach a 2.4x reduction
Asks who specifically owns the requirement behind the current output spec (rendition ladder, codec, quality settings), by person rather than by team
Orders the recommended actions by size of cost contribution rather than by ease of implementation
Names which stage of the question/delete/simplify/accelerate/automate ordering each recommendation belongs to, instead of presenting one undifferentiated list

evals.name: scope-cut-under-deadline
evals.prompt: We committed to shipping a rebuilt onboarding flow in 6 weeks. We're 3 weeks in and realistically about 30% done. The spec has 14 required profile fields, email + SMS verification, a manual document-review step for business accounts, and a 5-screen guided tour. My PM is asking me what we cut. I need to give her an answer tomorrow morning.
evals.expected_output: Questions each requirement and asks who owns it, proposes an explicit deletion list before any optimization, predicts what will need to be added back, flags the document-review/verification items as potentially irreversible-failure items outside the delete-and-add-back loop, and gives a calibrated schedule alongside the aggressive one.
expectations: Produces an explicit deletion list of named spec items before proposing any optimization, parallelization, or 'ship it faster' suggestions
Asks for the named individual behind at least one requirement (who required 14 fields, who required the guided tour) and rejects department-level attribution such as 'product wants it'
Predicts which cut items are likely to be added back later, rather than presenting the cuts as permanent
Flags at least one item (business-account document review, or verification) as carrying irreversible or compliance/fraud-risk failure and treats it differently from the freely deletable items
Gives a calibrated schedule estimate derived from the observed throughput (30% in 3 weeks) alongside any aggressive target, rather than only asserting the 6-week date can be met
Does not recommend automating or optimizing any step it has not first tested for deletion
Names which stage of the question/delete/simplify/accelerate/automate ordering each recommendation belongs to, instead of presenting one undifferentiated list

evals.name: build-vs-buy-bottleneck
evals.prompt: We pay a vendor $180k/yr for our product search API and their p99 is around 800ms, which is genuinely hurting conversion on our biggest page. A couple of the senior engineers keep floating building our own on OpenSearch. Honestly I can't tell if that's engineering ego or if they're right, and I have to take a recommendation to my VP next week.
evals.expected_output: Establishes whether search is actually the bottleneck, derives a latency floor for the query workload and computes the multiple against 800ms, separates the latency problem from the cost problem, applies own-the-bottleneck reasoning without defaulting to 'build it', and names the failure modes (schedule optimism on the build, ownership costs) with counter-checks.
expectations: Questions whether search latency is actually the dominant contributor to the conversion problem before evaluating build-vs-buy
Derives a latency floor for this query workload (from index size, query type, or comparable achievable p99) and compares it to the observed 800ms as an explicit multiple or gap
Separates the $180k/yr cost question from the 800ms latency question and notes they may have different answers
Considers options between 'stay' and 'build' (caching, pushing the vendor on latency, narrowing what search is asked to do) rather than framing the decision as binary
Applies own-the-bottleneck reasoning explicitly: recommends in-housing only if search is confirmed to be the rate-limiting constraint, not because vendors are bad
Names schedule optimism on the build estimate as a risk and supplies a concrete counter-check, rather than only listing pros and cons
Names which stage of the question/delete/simplify/accelerate/automate ordering each recommendation belongs to, instead of presenting one undifferentiated list
